Summary · Evaluation · Appraisal

Explainable temporal machine learning of multimorbidity trajectories after acute myocardial infarction: complementing clinical risk scores with mechanistic phenotypes

Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association · Research and Applications · 2026 · DOI: 10.1093/jamia/ocag135

Primary-source appraisal of a retrospective UK Biobank study combining temporal clustering, topic modeling, supervised classification, SHAP interpretation, survival analysis, PheWAS, and Reactome enrichment after acute myocardial infarction.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis: Longitudinal post-AMI diagnosis sequences can be clustered into clinically interpretable multimorbidity trajectories, and those trajectory labels can be predicted to some degree from pre-AMI data. The trajectories add phenotypic and mechanistic description, but only small incremental mortality discrimination beyond SMART and no independent trajectory effect after full adjustment.
Trajectory discovery
3 profiles: ACUTE-CARD 63.4% (n=8,052), CARDIOMIX 13.5% (n=1,720), SMO-CARD 23.1% (n=2,929).
Internal prediction
XGBoost AUC-ROC 0.906 (95% CI 0.895-0.916), weighted F1 0.782, weighted accuracy 0.789.
Leakage sensitivity
When the final 7 days before AMI were excluded, XGBoost AUC-ROC fell to 0.635 (95% CI 0.617-0.652).
Mortality
5-year all-cause mortality: 12.8% ACUTE-CARD, 20.6% CARDIOMIX, 43.9% SMO-CARD.
Incremental prognosis
C-index 0.59 trajectory alone; 0.65 SMART alone; 0.67 trajectory + SMART. Trajectory effects became non-significant after full adjustment.
Mechanistic layer
Profile-specific PheWAS / pathway enrichment patterns were reported, but the analysis is associative and does not establish causal mechanisms.
Major source-level consistency problem: Figure 1 labels CatBoost as the “Best Model” with AUC-ROC 0.77 and weighted accuracy 65%, while the Results and Figure 3 report XGBoost as highest-discrimination model with AUC-ROC 0.906 and weighted accuracy 0.789; CatBoost is reported at AUC-ROC 0.900 and accuracy 0.773. The main-text narrative and Figure 3 are internally concordant, but Figure 1 is not.

Section condensation

Abstract

The authors set out to identify post-AMI multimorbidity trajectories using explainable temporal machine learning and to test their clinical, prognostic, and biological significance. Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) k-means was used on post-AMI diagnostic sequences in 12,701 UK Biobank participants; LDA characterized cluster themes; four multiclass models predicted cluster membership from pre-AMI diagnoses and demographics; SHAP explained predictors; SMART plus Cox models assessed 5-year mortality; and PheWAS/Reactome analyses were used to seek profile-specific biological signals.

The abstract reports three trajectories, strong internal multiclass discrimination for XGBoost (AUC-ROC 0.906), highest 5-year mortality in SMO-CARD (43.9%), and SMART as the dominant mortality predictor. Its central claim is therefore not that the trajectory model replaces SMART, but that it provides complementary phenotypic and mechanistic information.

Introduction

The rationale is that static comorbidity counts lose temporal ordering and spacing. The paper positions DTW as a way to compare sequences progressing at different speeds and SHAP/topic modeling as ways to make the resulting machine-learning pipeline clinically interpretable.

The authors hypothesize that temporal clustering will produce clinically interpretable and biologically distinct trajectories, that cluster membership can be predicted from pre-AMI information, and that the trajectories will complement conventional risk scores. This is an exploratory/discovery framing rather than a prespecified clinical decision-impact study.

Methods - study design and diagnostic processing

This retrospective cohort used UK Biobank application 83,988. Eligibility required incident AMI (ICD-10 I21), at least 5 years of follow-up or death within that window, complete demographic data, and plausible dates. Hospital inpatient ICD-10 diagnoses were filtered, rare codes removed, and remaining codes truncated to three characters, producing 1,008 distinct codes. Diagnoses were separated into a pre-AMI window of 365 to 1 days before AMI and a post-AMI window of 0 to 5 years.

The use of hospital inpatient codes means the trajectory representation is a record of coded hospital diagnoses, not a complete longitudinal disease state. The main text later acknowledges that primary-care conditions and sub-annual dynamics are missed despite UK Biobank's broader record linkage.

Methods - temporal representation and clustering

Post-AMI diagnoses were encoded as age-indexed binary matrices, with ICD-10 codes as rows and integer ages as columns; a 1 marks first occurrence and 0 otherwise. Ages were standardized. The authors explicitly chose age indexing over time-since-AMI to capture age-dependent disease susceptibility. DTW k-means (tslearn 0.6.3) was tested over k=2-9; k=3 was selected using elbow, silhouette, and Davies-Bouldin criteria.

This representation preserves temporal gaps but collapses repeated coded events after first occurrence and therefore does not directly model recurrence, persistence, dosage/intensity, or changing severity. The age-indexing choice is clinically motivated but is also a modeling assumption that may entangle chronological age with post-event time.

Methods - cluster characterization

LDA (two topics per cluster) was applied within each DTW cluster to binary post-AMI diagnosis vectors, treating patient records as documents and ICD codes as words. Two clinicians grouped top codes into clinical categories and assigned labels; agreement was high (Cohen's kappa 0.939; 95% agreement across 60 codes, four minor disagreements). Co-occurrence networks used Pearson correlations among binary indicators, retaining edges above the 95th percentile.

The clinician labeling step improves interpretability but also introduces a post hoc semantic layer on top of data-driven clusters. The paper does not present a separate validation set for the labels themselves beyond reviewer agreement.

Methods - supervised prediction and SHAP

Pre-AMI diagnoses were mapped to 27 ICD-10-based clinical categories and combined with age, sex, BMI, and Index of Multiple Deprivation. Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost were tuned with 3-fold cross-validation using weighted F1, inverse-frequency class weights, and an 80/20 stratified train/test split. SHAP values were calculated for the best model. A key sensitivity analysis repeated prediction after excluding the final seven days before AMI.

Performance uncertainty was estimated by 1,000 bootstrap resamples. This is good internal validation practice, but the study has no external cohort and the dramatic sensitivity decline after removing near-event diagnoses indicates that the headline discrimination depends heavily on information immediately preceding AMI.

Methods - survival and biological analyses

Four Cox models compared trajectory membership, SMART, trajectory + SMART, and a fully adjusted model additionally including age, sex, IMD, SBP, diabetes, prior CAD, cerebrovascular disease, and PAD. Discrimination used Harrell's C-index; Kaplan-Meier curves provided unadjusted separation. The main text states that SMART was calculated at AMI incidence using UK Biobank baseline variables, but it does not fully clarify the temporal alignment of those baseline measurements with the index event.

PheWAS mapped cluster conditions to PheCodes and tested SNP associations with adjustment for age, sex, ancestry principal components, and genotyping array; FDR-significant SNPs were used for Reactome enrichment. These analyses are associative and exploratory. The main article gives counts and pathway themes but not the detailed effect-size landscape needed to evaluate biological specificity independently.

Results - cohort and trajectories

Five-year all-cause mortality was 21.0% (2,673 deaths). The text reports median age at AMI of 69 years (IQR 63-74) and 30.9% male; Table 1, labeled as baseline characteristics, reports median age 62 years (56-66), consistent with measurements occurring earlier in UK Biobank follow-up. Participants had a median of eight post-AMI diagnoses and four diagnoses in the pre-AMI year.

Three clusters were reported: ACUTE-CARD (63.4%), characterized by early cardiometabolic disease plus episodic cardiorespiratory decompensation; CARDIOMIX (13.5%), with structural cardiac, arrhythmic, valvular, and cardiorenal-metabolic burden; and SMO-CARD (23.1%), with progressive respiratory/frailty/multisystem disease. SMO-CARD participants were older and more deprived and had the highest 5-year mortality.

Results - prediction

XGBoost had the highest reported main-window discrimination: AUC-ROC 0.906 (95% CI 0.895-0.916), weighted F1 0.782, macro F1 0.713, and weighted accuracy 0.789. CatBoost was comparable at AUC-ROC 0.900 (95% CI 0.889-0.910), weighted F1 0.780, macro F1 0.732, and accuracy 0.773. SMO-CARD was the most distinct class, while ACUTE-CARD and CARDIOMIX were more commonly confused.

SHAP patterns aligned with the assigned phenotypes: respiratory diagnoses and higher deprivation favored SMO-CARD; atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, and diabetes favored CARDIOMIX; hypertension and dyslipidemia without respiratory markers favored ACUTE-CARD. Crucially, excluding the seven days immediately before AMI reduced XGBoost AUC-ROC to 0.635 (95% CI 0.617-0.652), sharply weakening the claim that durable pre-event history alone predicts later trajectory membership.

Results - mortality and SMART

Trajectory membership alone had modest discrimination (C-index 0.59). SMART alone performed better (0.65), and trajectory + SMART reached 0.67. In the fully adjusted model, trajectory effects attenuated to non-significance. Thus, the paper's strongest supported prognostic conclusion is that the clusters separate unadjusted risk and add only marginal discrimination beyond SMART.

The authors interpret the trajectories as complementary because they describe how risk factors cluster across organ systems, not because they materially outperform SMART. The supplementary Kaplan-Meier and Cox details referenced in Figure S1/Table S5 were not available in the uploaded PDF.

Results - genetic associations and pathway enrichment

The paper reports 2,839, 2,913, and 2,808 significant SNPs for ACUTE-CARD, CARDIOMIX, and SMO-CARD, respectively. ACUTE-CARD is described as enriched for innate immune/chemokine/extracellular-matrix pathways; CARDIOMIX for insulin signaling, lipid transport, and atrial conduction; and SMO-CARD for chronic inflammatory, connective-tissue, and smoking-related degenerative pathways.

The authors call these signals evidence that the clusters capture genuine pathophysiological differences. That wording is stronger than the design can establish: enrichment can show biological coherence or hypothesis-generating association, but it does not independently validate the causal pathophysiology of a data-derived trajectory.

Discussion and clinical implications

The discussion emphasizes that temporal ordering adds information beyond static comorbidity counts and that explainability can make the phenotypes clinically intelligible. The authors propose different potential intervention priorities for the profiles - pulmonary/geriatric evaluation for SMO-CARD, arrhythmia/nephrology attention for CARDIOMIX, and cardiometabolic optimization for ACUTE-CARD.

Those intervention suggestions are plausible phenotype-driven hypotheses, not tested treatment effects. The authors themselves state that validation in diverse populations and prospective implementation studies are required before clinical deployment.

Limitations, strengths, and conclusion

Stated limitations include UK Biobank healthy-participant selection bias, predominantly White British composition, hospital ICD-10 dependence, missing primary-care/sub-annual dynamics, and the observational design. Strengths include scale, long follow-up, multi-metric clustering checks, explainable supervised learning, and integrative genomic analyses. Code is reported as publicly available; individual-level UK Biobank data remain access controlled.

The conclusion that the workflow is a reproducible template for mechanistically informed longitudinal phenotyping is reasonable as a methodological proposition. The stronger claims that the profiles are biologically “grounded” or ready to support precision care should be read cautiously because external validation, prospective utility, and causal mechanistic validation are absent.

Figures, table, and workflow extraction

Figure 1 - analytical workflow

Purpose: End-to-end analytical pipeline.
Inputs: UK Biobank EHR; incident AMI cohort; ICD-10 diagnoses; demographics; SMART variables; genotype data.
Process: pre/post windows → age-indexed diagnosis sequences → DTW k-means → LDA/network characterization → supervised classifier + SHAP → Cox/SMART comparison → PheWAS/pathway enrichment.
Outputs: 3 trajectory profiles, pre-AMI prediction, survival associations, pathway signatures.
Failure modes: near-AMI information dependence; single-cohort validation; diagnostic coding limitations; associative biological interpretation.
Critical inconsistency: figure labels CatBoost as best model (AUC-ROC 0.77, weighted accuracy 65%), conflicting with Results/Figure 3.

Table 1 - baseline characteristics by profile

Whole cohort: n=12,701; 69.1% female; baseline age median 62 (56,66); SMART 11.8 (9.1,15.2).
ACUTE-CARD: n=8,052; all-cause mortality 12.8%; SMART 11.2 (8.9,14.2); eGFR 91 (81,101).
CARDIOMIX: n=1,720; all-cause mortality 20.6%; SMART 11.2 (8.8,14.8); CAD 14.8%.
SMO-CARD: n=2,929; all-cause mortality 43.9%; SMART 14.0 (10.4,18.4); eGFR 85 (73,96); diabetes 15.7%; CAD 22.6%; PAD 3.9%.
Appraisal: broad baseline differences indicate that the clusters capture major differences in age/comorbidity/deprivation; these same factors also explain much of the mortality gradient.

Figure 2 - DTW cluster selection and profile themes

Purpose: justify k and summarize cluster content.
Panels: elbow SSE; silhouette score; Davies-Bouldin index; LDA-derived clinical-category heatmap; profile sizes.
Key values: k=3; silhouette 0.45; Davies-Bouldin 0.85; cluster sizes 8,052 / 1,720 / 2,929.
Pattern: k=3 maximizes silhouette and yields interpretable, imbalanced profiles.
Limit: cluster-number choice is not uniquely determined by every diagnostic metric; reproducibility in other cohorts is untested.

Figure 3 - supervised profile prediction

Logistic regression: AUC-ROC 0.901; weighted F1 0.773; accuracy 0.765.
Random forest: AUC-ROC 0.892; weighted F1 0.767; accuracy 0.778.
XGBoost: AUC-ROC 0.906 (95% CI 0.895-0.916); weighted F1 0.782; accuracy 0.789.
CatBoost: AUC-ROC 0.900 (95% CI 0.889-0.910); weighted F1 0.780; accuracy 0.773.
Main limitation: the separate leakage-sensitivity analysis drops XGBoost AUC-ROC to 0.635 after excluding the final 7 pre-AMI days.

Figure 4 - SHAP, co-occurrence networks, and pathway enrichment

Purpose: supply interpretability and biological context for the three profiles.
SHAP: profile predictions are driven by clinically recognizable combinations of ischemic, arrhythmic, respiratory, renal, metabolic, age, BMI, and deprivation features.
Networks: ACUTE-CARD emphasizes cardiometabolic/cardiac failure hubs; CARDIOMIX shows cardiorenal-metabolic structure; SMO-CARD has respiratory/frailty/multisystem hubs.
Pathways: immune/interleukin/PI3K-related signals overlap across profiles with profile-specific emphasis.
Appraisal: these panels improve descriptive coherence, but they do not establish that the clusters are causal disease mechanisms or that acting on the SHAP features will alter outcomes.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read soon. The paper is a useful methodological example of longitudinal EHR phenotyping and explainable multimodal validation, especially because its own sensitivity analysis exposes how much apparent predictive performance can depend on diagnoses recorded immediately before the index event. It is not ready to guide clinical care or deployment.
Relevance
9/10

Strong fit for clinical informatics, longitudinal phenotyping, explainability, and risk-model complementarity.

Evidence basis: full temporal + prediction + survival + biological pipeline. Limiting factor: AMI-specific case study. Would rise: demonstration across multiple diseases/settings.

Novelty
7/10

The integration is novel/useful, although DTW, LDA, SHAP, boosted trees, Cox models, PheWAS, and enrichment are established methods.

Evidence basis: unusual end-to-end combination. Limiting factor: novelty is primarily architectural/integrative. Would rise: clear evidence that temporal representation itself materially improves external performance or clinical utility.

Method strength
6/10

Large cohort, explicit clustering diagnostics, internal train/test split, bootstrap CIs, and leakage sensitivity are strengths.

Limiting factor: single cohort, no external validation, first-occurrence coding representation, unclear time alignment for some SMART inputs, and a major figure-level performance inconsistency. Would rise: preregistered/external replication and reconciliation of reporting.

Evidence strength
5/10

Evidence supports descriptive trajectory discovery and internal association; it is weaker for durable pre-AMI prediction, incremental prognosis, and mechanistic claims.

Evidence basis: AUC 0.906 main window but 0.635 after removing 7 near-event days; C-index gain 0.65→0.67; trajectory effects non-significant after full adjustment. Would rise: external prediction, stable sensitivity analyses, mechanistic replication, and prospective outcomes.

External validity
4/10

Generalizability is limited by UK Biobank selection, predominantly White British participants, inpatient diagnosis coding, and lack of external validation.

Evidence basis: limitations explicitly acknowledged by authors. Would rise: CPRD/SAIL or multi-health-system replication with calibration and subgroup analysis.

Implementation value
6/10

Build-useful as a pipeline template; not deployment-useful as a clinical classifier.

Evidence basis: code availability, explicit methods, explainability, and pipeline diagram. Limiting factor: no prospective workflow study, decision-impact analysis, calibration, or external validation. Would rise: silent prospective validation and utility testing.

Main strengths

  • Large, longitudinal, deeply phenotyped cohort.
  • Explicit temporal representation rather than static comorbidity counts.
  • Multiple cluster-selection diagnostics and clinician review of phenotype labels.
  • Comparison of several supervised classifiers with bootstrap uncertainty.
  • Important near-event leakage sensitivity analysis.
  • Openly reported code repository and transparent data-access limitations.

Main limitations

  • No external or prospective validation.
  • Headline classifier performance depends heavily on the final week before AMI.
  • Trajectory adds only ~0.02 C-index over SMART and loses independent significance after full adjustment.
  • Hospital ICD codes and first-occurrence encoding simplify disease state and recurrence.
  • Biological enrichment is associative; “mechanistic validation” is overstated.
  • Figure 1 conflicts materially with Results/Figure 3 on the best model and performance.
  • Supplementary figures/tables needed for full audit were not supplied.
Do not use for: choosing patient-specific interventions, replacing SMART, assigning a clinical care pathway, or claiming causal biological mechanisms.
Best use: methodological reference for how to combine temporal clustering, post hoc phenotype labeling, interpretable prediction, risk-score comparison, and biological association - and as a cautionary example of why temporally strict leakage checks matter.

Implementation and research takeaways

What to reuse
The pipeline architecture: temporal clustering → interpretable phenotype labeling → supervised prediction → leakage sensitivity → conventional score comparison → biological hypothesis generation.
What to monitor
Strict temporal leakage, cluster stability, calibration, class-specific errors, and whether performance persists when near-index codes are removed.
What to change in a replication
Use external cohorts; preserve recurrent events; compare age indexing with time-since-event; predefine cluster selection; add calibration and decision-curve analysis.
What not to overclaim
SHAP is not causality; pathway enrichment is not mechanistic proof; unadjusted mortality separation is not independent prognostic value; internal AUC is not deployment readiness.
Highest-value result
The sensitivity analysis: removing only the final 7 days before AMI reduces XGBoost AUC from 0.906 to 0.635, exposing dependence on near-event information.
Next evidence needed
External replication in representative EHR cohorts, prospective silent validation, stability analyses, and a trial or quasi-experimental evaluation of trajectory-guided care.
